questions.q: What does the Single Responsibility Principle say?
o: A class should have one reason to change
A class should contain only one method
A class should have only one field
A class should have only one caller
questions.w: "Responsibility" means a reason to change, such as business rules versus persistence. It is not a method count.

questions.q: A `ReportService` has a long `if/else` over report types and you edit it for every new type. Which principle does this violate?
o: Open-Closed: extend behaviour instead of editing existing code
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
Dependency Inversion
questions.w: Introduce a `ReportGenerator` interface and a class per type, for example with the Strategy pattern, so new types do not touch old code.

questions.q: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require?
o: A subtype must work wherever the base type is expected
A subclass must override every inherited method
A base class must always be abstract
A subtype must add more fields than its base
questions.w: A subtype must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions. A `ReadOnlyList` that throws on `add` breaks it.

questions.q: An interface `Worker` has `work()`, `eat()` and `sleep()`, and a `Robot` has to implement `eat()` with an exception. Which principle is violated?
o: Interface Segregation: don't depend on methods you don't use
Single Responsibility
Open-Closed
Liskov Substitution alone
questions.w: Split into smaller role interfaces such as `Workable` and `Feedable`. Classes then implement only what applies to them.

o: High-level code should depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
Low-level code should call high-level code directly
All dependencies should be made static
Classes should create their own dependencies
questions.w: The business service depends on a `PaymentGateway` interface and the concrete implementation is supplied from outside.

questions.q: How does Spring's dependency injection support Dependency Inversion?
o: The container supplies implementations, so classes see only interfaces
It turns every bean into a static singleton in the JVM
It hides every interface from the developers who use it
It generates the business logic itself from the configuration
questions.w: Constructor injection of an interface makes classes easy to test with fakes, and implementations easy to swap.

questions.q: A `UserService` builds emails, writes to the database and formats PDF statements. What is the most sensible fix?
o: Split it into focused classes, one per reason to change
Add more methods with clearer names
Make the class final so nobody extends it
Move everything into a static utility class
questions.w: Separate notification, persistence and reporting so a change in one does not risk the others.

questions.q: Is applying every SOLID principle to the extreme always good?
o: No, over-abstraction adds complexity, so apply them where change happens
Yes, because adding more interfaces is always an improvement
Yes, every single class in the codebase needs its own interface
No, because the principles only apply to Java code and nothing else
questions.w: Principles are guidelines. Premature abstraction creates indirection with no benefit. Refactor when a second variation appears.
